extracted.intended_audience: stakeholders participating in Title IX rulemaking (members of the public submitting comments), recipients of Federal financial assistance (educational institutions), and administrative/policy practitioners advising on notice-and-comment and Title IX compliance
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and responses in the Title IX final-rule preamble about how the Department handled the NPRM, what commenters may expect (posting, timing, scope, and review), and what recipients must do to prepare for and implement the final regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious-exemption scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute's religious exemption applies to educational institutions controlled by a religious organization; it does not exempt student organizations, individual employees or students, or educational institutions not controlled by religious organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent with § 106.6(d)(1), nothing in the final regulations requires or authorizes a recipient to infringe on individuals' First Amendment or other constitutional rights. The intersection of the prohibition on sex-based harassment with First Amendment rights is addressed in the definition of sex-based harassment in § 106.2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay within NPRM scope / separate rulemakings for out-of-scope regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department did not request comments on 34 CFR 75.500(d) or 76.500(d) in the July 2022 NPRM because they are outside the scope of this rulemaking; the Department proposed rescinding those regulations in a separate rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should not attempt to address or rescind regulations outside the scope of the published NPRM; such actions require separate notice-and-comment proceedings (see separate rulemaking referenced at 88 FR 10857).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiated-rulemaking requirements apply only where statutorily required
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 492 of the HEA (negotiated rulemaking) applies exclusively to regulations that implement Title IV of the HEA; Title IX is not part of the HEA and thus is not subject to those negotiated-rulemaking requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not required by HEA negotiated rulemaking, agencies should still solicit live and written comments, hold public hearings, and conduct listening sessions as appropriate to gather stakeholder input; the Department did so (June 2021 Public Hearing, listening sessions, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interagency review and consultation (OMB and DOJ)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consistent with Executive Order 12866, the Department coordinated with other agencies by sharing the proposed regulations with the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) prior to publication; in accordance with Executive Order 12250, the Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights at DOJ reviewed the proposed regulations and approved them for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should use interagency review (via OMB) to give other Federal agencies opportunity to review and comment; consult DOJ on civil-rights-related regulations as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advisory groups are discretionary, not required
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department acknowledged suggestions to create a standing advisory group but concluded the public hearing, listening sessions, and notice-and-comment process provided sufficient opportunity for input; nothing in final regulations precludes recipients from creating their own advisory groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may create advisory groups but are not required to do so when robust public engagement has occurred; recipients may form their own advisory groups to assist with implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use separate NPRMs for complex or unique topics (e.g., athletics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because athletics present unique considerations, the Department noted proposed § 106.31(a)(2) would not apply to sex-separate athletic team eligibility and that a separate NPRM (the Athletics NPRM) would clarify Title IX's application to athletic eligibility criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When issues are interrelated but require distinct analysis (e.g., athletics eligibility), agencies should issue separate NPRMs to ensure full consideration of the range of views and technical issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a meaningful opportunity to comment (length of comment period)
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA requires agencies to give interested persons an opportunity to participate in the proceedings; this has generally been interpreted as requiring a 'meaningful opportunity to comment.' Case law generally concludes that comment periods should not be less than 30 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department provided a 60-day comment period for the July 2022 NPRM and declined requests to extend, noting the volume and detailed nature of comments (over 240,000). Agencies should consider extending comment periods when submission difficulties exist or when additional time is required for meaningful participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accommodations and assistance for submitting comments
rubrics_metrics.description: When a commenter had difficulty submitting comments through Regulations.gov, the Department provided information regarding the Regulations.gov help desk and accepted written comments via mail and email for those who requested an accommodation or could not otherwise submit comments online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should provide assistance and alternative submission methods (mail, email) when members of the public experience difficulty using the electronic comment system, and consult with the system administrator (GSA) if widespread problems are reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tracking and posting comments; two narrow exceptions to public posting
rubrics_metrics.description: When a commenter submits a comment on Regulations.gov, they receive a tracking number. The Department made all material available for public viewing on Regulations.gov with two exceptions: (1) portions of comments containing personally identifiable information about someone other than the commenter, and (2) comments that contained threats of harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should review comments before posting, redact PII about third parties, withhold threats of harm, and post comments otherwise in their entirety to promote transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of comment tallies and multi-signature submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: A single comment submission can include a self-reported number of signatories; in one instance a single submission inaccurately reported 201,303 submissions. The Department identified the error and GSA corrected the number of submissions for that comment to one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies and the system administrator should ensure accurate counting of comments and correct obvious errors in self-reported tallies of multi-signature submissions; public tallies are generated by GSA's Regulations.gov.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review and consideration of all submitted comments
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department reviewed and considered all comments submitted during the comment period, including duplicate comments and comments that contained threats of harm or personally identifiable information (though threats and third-party PII were not posted publicly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should evaluate and consider all material submitted during the comment period, even if some submissions are duplicates or contain disallowed content that must be redacted or withheld from public posting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective date timing and non-retroactivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the APA, the effective date for final regulations cannot be fewer than 30 days after publication unless a statutory exception applies. The Department set the effective date of these final regulations to August 1, 2024 (more than 90 days after publication). The Department will not enforce these final regulations retroactively; final regulations apply only to sex discrimination that allegedly occurred on or after August 1, 2024.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should set an effective date that provides recipients time to prepare (commonly at least 30 days, often 60), and refrain from retroactive application absent express statutory authority; for conduct before the effective date evaluate compliance against the rules in effect at the time of the conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide technical assistance during transition
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department understands recipients may need technical assistance between publication and the effective date and after the regulations become effective, and the Department will offer technical assistance, as appropriate, to promote compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should plan to provide technical assistance to regulated entities during implementation and transition periods to facilitate compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on mandating student-facing curriculum or prevention programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Although commenters requested the Department require student-facing education and prevention programming, the Department declined to require such practices aside from § 106.8(d) (training for individuals responsible for implementing the regulations). Because the Department does not control school curricula, it declines to add requirements that recipients instruct students on sex-based harassment prevention or sex education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should avoid imposing curriculum mandates on educational institutions through civil-rights regulations; recipients retain discretion to provide educational programming they deem appropriate; funding for such programs lies with Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal authority over recipients receiving federal funds (Tenth Amendment/federalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department concluded these final regulations do not violate the Tenth Amendment; in exchange for Federal funds, recipients agree to comply with Title IX and related regulations, and the Federal government retains authority to regulate sex discrimination in education programs or activities that receive Federal financial assistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When regulating entities that accept federal funds, agencies may condition receipt of funds on compliance with nondiscrimination requirements, while recognizing traditional state authority in education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory delegation of rulemaking authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 20 U.S.C. 1682, agencies authorized to extend Federal financial assistance are empowered and directed to effectuate Title IX (20 U.S.C. 1681) by issuing rules, regulations, or orders of general applicability to achieve the objectives of the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should ground regulatory authority in the relevant statutory delegation (here 20 U.S.C. 1682) and may enforce compliance through termination or refusal to grant assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to require remedies to effectuate Title IX
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department disagrees with commenters who asserted that it lacks authority to require recipients to end all forms of sexual harassment and provide remedies; the authority extends to requiring remedies because such remedies eliminate the harm of sex-based harassment and prevent its recurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations that impose remedial requirements may be appropriate to effectuate statutory nondiscrimination mandates when they are necessary to eliminate discrimination and prevent recurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with Executive Orders and use of qualitative benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department complied with Executive Orders 12866 and 14021 by identifying the problem and assessing its significance. Agencies are not generally required to produce empirical evidence; Executive Order 12866 and OMB guidance allow consideration of qualitative benefits and prophylactic rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing need for regulation, agencies should consider case law, enforcement experience, stakeholder feedback, and both quantitative and qualitative benefits; agencies may adopt prophylactic rules without waiting for full empirical data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for long-lasting but flexible regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters requested long-lasting regulations to provide settled expectations and to avoid frequent changes that impose costs on institutions; the Department recognized concerns about shifting regulatory landscapes and resource burdens from frequent updates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should balance durability and flexibility when drafting regulations to provide settled expectations while retaining the ability to respond to changing circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recusal/disqualification standard for agency officials involved in rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency member should be disqualified only when there has been a clear and convincing showing that the agency member has an 'unalterably closed mind' on matters critical to the proceeding. Mere prior advocacy or expressions of opinion do not, without more, show that an agency member cannot maintain an open mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenges to agency officials' participation in rulemaking must meet a high standard; pre-proposal statements or prior advocacy are generally insufficient to require recusal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain necessity of regulatory action (regulatory justification)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department provided the need for regulatory action in the July 2022 NPRM based on Federal case law under Title IX, enforcement experience, and stakeholder feedback gathered during public hearings and listening sessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should document the problem they intend to address and the basis for regulatory action (legal precedents, enforcement experience, stakeholder input), and include analysis of costs and benefits (see Regulatory Impact Analysis).
